title: ⭐ Practice: what the offer really includes

questions.prompt: Sami is booking a week in a hotel and does not want to pay for a single meal on top of the price of the room. Which line does he tick on the booking form?

options.text: half board
full board
single room
bed and breakfast

questions.explanation: Full board is the formula in which the price of the room includes every meal of the day, so nothing is left to pay at the table. Half board stops at breakfast and one other meal, which leaves the third to be paid for somewhere else, and bed and breakfast leaves two. As for a single room, it answers another question altogether: it says how many people sleep in the room, and not one word about food. A booking form asks both questions, and a traveller who confuses them eats at his own expense all week.

questions.prompt: The travel agent tells the group: "You check in at the hotel desk as soon as the coach arrives." What does the group do there?

options.text: They pay what is left of the price of the tour.
They leave their suitcases in a room until the evening.
They choose the excursions they would like to join.
They report their arrival and are given their rooms.

questions.explanation: To check in is to present yourself at a desk on arrival and receive what your booking entitles you to: at a hotel, the room and its key; at an airport, a boarding card in exchange for the suitcase you hand over. Paying a balance, storing luggage and signing up for excursions are all things that can happen in the same lobby on the same afternoon, but none of them is what the two words name. And at the end of the stay the opposite move has its own words: you check out.

questions.prompt: A museum pass is advertised in large letters — MUSEUM PASS: ALL SIX SITES, ONE PRICE — and at the foot of the page comes a line beginning with an asterisk. What is that asterisk there for?

options.text: It points to a condition that limits the promise above it.
It marks the line the museum most wants you to read.
It shows that the prices on the page may change next year.
It repeats, in smaller print, what the large letters say.

questions.explanation: The asterisk is the page's own footnote, and it always points the same way: upwards, at a promise, to take something back from it. All six sites, one price becomes all six sites except the temporary exhibition, and the exception is set in small type precisely because nobody would sign if it were set in large type. It never underlines the offer, it never announces a change of price, and it never repeats the line above — a footnote that repeated it would be worth nothing at all. Read the large letters to learn what is being offered, and the asterisk to learn what you will still be paying for.

questions.prompt: The word "separate" is said with three syllables when it is a verb, [ˈsepəreɪt], and with two when it is an adjective, [ˈseprət]. In which sentence is it said with three?

options.text: The evening concerts need a separate ticket.
Each of the groups travels to the site on a separate coach.
Please separate the hand luggage from the suitcases.
A separate desk is open for group bookings.

questions.explanation: Only the verb keeps its three syllables, and a verb is what the word is here: somebody is being asked to do something, to put the small bags on one side and the big ones on the other. In the three other sentences the word stands in front of a noun and describes it — a ticket, a coach, a desk — which makes it an adjective, and the adjective drops its middle syllable altogether: [ˈseprət], two beats, with a weak [ə] at the end. Decide what the word is doing in the sentence, and its pronunciation is decided with it.

questions.prompt: Your e-mail must do more than admire the offer: it has to bring an answer back. Which sentence asks the festival office for information?

options.text: Your group pass sounds interesting to all of us.
I'm keen on festivals of this kind, and always have been.
The programme you print in the magazine is interesting.
I'd like to know more about the craft exhibition.

questions.explanation: Of the five frames the lesson gives you, two put a question to your reader and oblige him to reply — I'd like to know more about…, Please tell me about… — while the others only place you. Saying that a pass sounds interesting, that you are keen on festivals or that a programme is worth reading is true, pleasant and completely unanswerable: the office can nod at all three and write nothing back. Interest opens the door; only a request walks through it.

questions.prompt: Sonia turns down the package tour: "I want to spend my third day in the old town, not in a coach going to the lake." Which drawback of a package tour is she naming?

options.text: The agency fixes the programme, and you follow it.
The group is too large to move quickly.
The whole price is paid before you leave home.
The hotel is often far from the centre of the town.

questions.explanation: What Sonia wants is her own third day, and a package tour is exactly the formula that hands the programme to somebody else: the agency has already chosen the lake, the coach and the hour, and the single price she paid covers all three. That is the drawback the lesson sets against the advantages — one payment, everything arranged, a guide who knows the way. The size of the group, the moment of payment and the position of the hotel are real drawbacks too, but she has complained about none of them: she is not saying the tour is slow, or dear, or badly placed. She is saying that the day is not hers.
